tracks.title: The blessed-vendor trap
tracks.text: Lesson seven point six — recipes. A sub-lesson, under wbx. Here's the trap every deploy tool you've used falls into. The list of clouds it can deploy to is baked into the binary. Fly, Render, a handful of blessed targets — each one a panel in the compiled tool. [curious] And if you want a cloud that isn't on the list? You wait for the maintainers… or you fork the whole CLI and recompile. Where to deploy was a decision the binary made for you, at compile time. This lesson is about a tool that made the opposite choice. The binary knows nothing about your cloud. It only knows how to find a recipe… and run it. Adding a cloud is a make-directory and an editor. No recompile. No pull request. No waiting.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: So what is a recipe? A recipe is one shell file — bootstrap dot sh — living at providers, slash, the name of your place. It sources a neutral spine. It fills five hooks, plus a lifecycle trio. It sets its place name… and calls one function. And by simply existing, that file becomes a deploy target — with no change to the compiled tool. [curious] Think of it as the engine contract, written as shell. Run my container… attach my volume… set my secrets… expose my port. Nothing more. The simplified model has no ephemeral sandbox half to manage — one container, with WebAssembly inside, and a platform to hold it. That narrow contract is exactly why sixty lines is enough.

tracks.title: Six actions, one case statement
tracks.text: Now the spine — six actions, one case statement. Every recipe sources one neutral file, and ends by calling wb recipe run. That function is the whole control flow — a single case statement, on one variable, with exactly six branches. Picture them fanning out. First, up — the full converge. Second, secrets — stage credentials, no deploy. Third, down. Fourth, status. Fifth, logs. Sixth, url. And anything the spine doesn't recognise falls through a trapdoor… and exits with code two. There is no seventh door. Now follow the up branch, because it expands into a chain. It assembles the engine environment first. Then it calls four hooks, in a fixed order — ensure the app exists… set the secrets… attach the volume… deploy the image. And it finishes by echoing the public url. [excited] That order is not negotiable, and that's the point. The spine owns the choreography, so no recipe has to. And the secrets action? It's the same machinery, used carefully — it runs only ensure-app and set-secrets. It hands a cloud your keys today… and ships the image next week. The two steps never have to happen together.

tracks.title: Five hooks and the trio
tracks.text: Next — five hooks and the trio. A recipe fills eight functions. Five hooks the converge calls, and three for the lifecycle. And the spine guarantees each one a clean stage. By the time a hook runs, the image is present, and the engine environment is already assembled. The house manner is one phrase — converge, don't complain. A hook gets run again and again, so it checks before it creates, and never errors on already there. Let me walk the five. First, ensure-app — the app exists after this runs. Fly does it in one line — fly status, or else fly apps create. Second, set-secrets — stage the whole environment on the platform. Third, attach-volume — durable storage at the data path. Fly creates a one-gigabyte volume, but only if it's missing. Fourth, deploy-image — the image running, the port exposed. And fifth, public-url — just print the reachable address. The verdict here is how thin each hook gets to be. Because the spine handed it a guaranteed image and a fixed call order… the author writes one line per concern, wrapping the platform's own command-line tool. The whole deploy-to-fly behaviour is six short functions. And the lifecycle trio — destroy, report, tail — maps one-to-one onto three more.

tracks.title: What the engine is told
tracks.text: What is the engine actually told? Before any hook runs, the spine builds the engine environment — the exact set of variables the deployed engine boots with. Five pairs are always there. First, web equals one — boot the control plane. Second, the port. Third, the data path. Fourth, the embed mode. And fifth — the load-bearing one — the registry, pointed at a file on the durable volume. Here's why that fifth one matters so much. The engine's default registry is in-memory. Fine for a laptop… fatal for a cloud that scales to zero. So the spine pins the registry to a file on the volume, and litestream replicates that database. [excited] The engine that wakes from sleep… is the engine that went to sleep. Every deployed workbook intact. After those five, a fixed list of axes — tenancy, storage, the S3 settings, the database url — is forwarded only if you set it. A minimal deploy ships a minimal environment. And one discipline, enforced by omission. The recipe never rotates a generated secret. The signing key, the public bearer — generated once, and persisted by you. Rotating them mid-flight would four-oh-one every live client and break the tenant's identity. A recipe that quietly re-rolled them… would be a recipe that quietly logged everyone out. So it doesn't.

tracks.title: Three rungs to find a recipe
tracks.text: If a provider is just a file, the only hard part is finding it. So — three rungs to find a recipe. The CLI tries them in order, and the first hit wins. Picture a ladder. Rung one… the environment. If you've set the providers-directory variable, that wins outright — point it anywhere, and that's your root. Rung two… the repo. From your working directory, the CLI walks up, looking for the spine file inside the deploy kit — that's how it works during development. And rung three… the standalone install. With neither of those, the CLI materializes the recipes it carries inside the binary itself. The spine and the fly recipe are baked into the compiled tool, so it writes them out under the app directory, and keeps them fresh by rewriting them every single run. [curious] That third rung is why the tool is self-contained. A fresh install — no repo, no environment variable — still has a working fly recipe, because the binary is carrying a copy. And to the CLI, a provider exists if, and only if, its bootstrap file is really there. The check is that literal. Run deploy doctor, and it scans for bootstrap files and lists what it finds — so you can confirm a recipe is seen, before you trust it.

tracks.title: The sealed spawn
tracks.text: Now the part that makes shelling out to a cloud safe to do — the sealed spawn. The CLI does not run your recipe in your shell. It runs it under env dash i — a sealed, empty environment — and hands in only an explicit allowlist. Your stray exports… your other API keys… your dot-env file. None of it leaks into a cloud deploy. Because the recipe's process starts with nothing… and receives only what the kit decided to give it. Picture the handoff as a sequence. First, the kit reads your declared secret values — from the staged secrets store first, your environment as a fallback. Second, it launches the recipe under env dash i, with a nine-name allowlist. The path, the home directory, the action, the providers directory, the image, the app name, the port, the region, and the list of secret key names. Third, the recipe assembles its environment from exactly that, and shells out to the platform tool. And fourth, its exit code is honored all the way back up. [excited] The allowlist isn't a precaution layered on top. It is the entire interface between your machine and the recipe. Two details earn their place. The home directory is on the list on purpose — it's how the fly tool finds its own auth token. The recipe never sees your fly credentials… the platform tool does. And the secret store at rest is written six-hundred — owner-only. List your secrets, and you get names, never values. Credentials move by name… until the last possible moment. And the last moment is sealed.

tracks.title: The bundled recipe, read whole
tracks.text: One recipe ships in the binary today — and its header states the stance in plain words. Fly is our personal preference, not a privileged target. Any platform gets its own bootstrap file, with the same hooks. It carries two strategies. The prebuilt path — the default — deploys your image by reference, no repo needed. And the app-build path — opt-in — builds from a repo using fly's remote builder, which is the path our own production engine takes. Let me read you what the prebuilt path writes, to a temporary directory, on every deploy… and then deletes. There is no fly config in your project, ever. The app name, my-workbooks-engine. The region, san jose. A build block, pointing at the runtime image. A mounts block — source wbdata, destination slash data. And an http-service block — internal port four thousand, force https true, auto-stop machines on, auto-start machines on… and minimum machines running… zero. Those last three lines are the economics. Minimum machines running zero means an idle engine costs almost nothing — it sleeps when no one's knocking, and wakes on the next request. And it wakes whole. Because the wbdata volume — one gigabyte, created only if it's absent — holds the registry database. [excited] The engine that wakes up is the engine that went to sleep. Scale-to-zero, plus a durable registry on a volume — that's the whole reason the registry was pinned off in-memory, two sections ago. The rest of the recipe is one-liners. The public url hook is literally an echo of https, the app name, dot fly dot dev. And the lifecycle trio is three thin fly calls.

tracks.title: Write a provider this afternoon
tracks.text: So let's write one. Suppose your cloud is Digital Ocean's app platform, driven by its tool, doctl. A provider for it is a single file. Let me read you the shape. A shebang line. Set the safety flags. Source the spine from the providers directory. Export the place name — droplet. Then a guard — if doctl isn't found, print a message and exit. And then the eight functions. Ensure-app lists the apps and creates one if yours is missing. Set-secrets updates the app with the environment pairs. Attach-volume is a no-op — the volume's declared in the app spec. Deploy-image creates a deployment. Public-url reads the default ingress. And the trio — delete, get, logs. The last line… calls wb recipe run. Now the before-and-after, because that's the whole pitch. Before the file exists, run deploy validate, and it bails with the exact path it wanted — no provider recipe for droplet, expected providers slash droplet slash bootstrap dot sh. So you set the providers-directory variable to point at your own folder. Run deploy doctor — and now it lists droplet, beside fly. Run deploy apply — and it deploys, through your recipe. [excited] One caveat the failure message names. The providers-directory variable replaces the search root — that's rung one — so your folder needs a copy of the spine beside your droplet recipe. The spine and your recipe live together. That's the entire ceremony. No fork. No recompile. No waiting on anyone. And your cloud is now a first-class target… on a tool you didn't change a line of.

tracks.title: One seam, three drivers
tracks.text: Now the proof the seam is real, rather than decorative — one seam, three drivers. The same bootstrap file is executed by three different callers. Picture three arrows, all converging on one file. The first arrow — the Rust CLI, when you run deploy apply. The second arrow — the runtime's Elixir backend, which spawns the same file through a system command, and honors its exit code, so the agent-experience exit contract reaches all the way down to the shell. And the third arrow — our own production CI, which exports the action and our build overrides and runs the very same fly recipe. [excited] The brandnana production engine is deployed through the exact recipe a kit user runs. One deploy path… dogfooded. The backend's own comment puts the seam plainly. Adding a provider is dropping a directory. The core never changes.

tracks.title: Where the recipe ends
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the recipe ends. The model is small on purpose, and the edges are real. First — one recipe ships today. The providers directory holds the spine, and fly. Every other cloud is a recipe someone writes. The seam is general… the library is one entry long. Second — a recipe shells out to the provider's own tool. So that tool must be installed and authenticated. The recipe checks, and tells you with the install link — but it can't conjure the tool. Third — secret values do reach the recipe's process environment, by design. That's how the engine gets configured. The mitigation is that the recipe is a shell script you can read in one screen, run sealed, with a known allowlist. There's no recipe registry, and no signing, yet. You're trusting a file you can audit — not a vendor's word. Fourth — local is not a recipe. It's a separate, built-in container seam, tried in order — docker, podman, then krunvm. And fifth — the contract presumes a platform shape. Something that can run container, volume, secrets, and port. A raw virtual machine with none of that means you build more inside the hooks. The seam doesn't shrink the work — it just gives it a fixed home.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I have to fork the repo to add a provider? No. Set the providers-directory variable to a folder of your own, drop your bootstrap file in beside a copy of the spine, and the CLI uses it. That's rung one — environment wins. Why bash, and not a real plugin API? Because a recipe's job is to call a cloud's own tool, and shell is the native language of calling tools. Sixty lines you can read beats a binary interface you can't. Where does fly get my API token? From the fly tool's own auth, by way of the home directory — which is on the spawn allowlist precisely so the platform tool can find its credentials. The recipe never handles your token. What if my platform has no volumes? Then attach-volume is where you solve it — bind whatever durable storage your platform offers to the data path, because the registry lives there, and must survive restarts. And — can a recipe rotate my bearer token? [chuckles] No, and that's deliberate. It's generated once, persisted, and never re-generated. Rotating it would four-oh-one every live client and break the tenant's identity. The recipe forwards it. It never re-rolls it.

tracks.title: Back up to wbx
tracks.text: So that's recipes. A cloud provider isn't code in the binary — it's a sixty-line shell file that fills five hooks and becomes a target by existing. The tool only finds it, and spawns it sealed. Fly isn't special — it's the one recipe that happens to ride along. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under wbx — lesson seven — the command line, and its deploy verb family. And the deploy kit lesson sits right beside this one — init, validate, apply — the ergonomics this seam lives behind. Read those, and the whole picture closes. A provider is a recipe… and a recipe is just a shell file.
